Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Vignette:
Mr. Raj Patel, a 61-year-old South Asian man, has been married for over three decades and works at a non-profit organization dedicated to community development. On his way home from work one evening last summer, Mr. Patel was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that left him with deep emotional scars. The accident occurred when another driver ran a red light, sending their car hurtling into the side of Mr. Patel's vehicle. The sheer force of the impact shattered the windows and sent shards of glass flying everywhere. The texture of the broken glass embedded in his clothes and skin is one that still haunts him today. To this day, any touch of rough or jagged surfaces immediately brings back vivid images from that night. Since the accident, Mr. Patel has become extremely vigilant about driving conditions and discussions around traffic accidents. Just hearing others talk about car crashes can trigger a cascade of unsettling memories and sensations. The sound of screeching tires or the sight of an accident on the news is enough to plunge him back into the traumatic event. He finds himself reliving those moments, his heart pounding as if the collision were happening all over again. Mr. Patel’s daily routine has become increasingly strained due to these triggers. As a non-profit worker, he often attends meetings and events that involve discussions about community safety, which frequently touch on traffic accidents. These conversations leave him feeling anxious and uncomfortable. He has started avoiding such gatherings or leaving them early to avoid exposure to potentially triggering topics. The tactile texture of broken glass is particularly distressing for Mr. Patel. Even the feel of rough paper or certain fabrics can set off a flashback, causing his body to tense up as if he were reliving the accident. This sensitivity affects his interactions at work, where he sometimes has difficulty focusing on tasks that involve handling such materials. Moreover, unexpected loud noises and sudden movements have become major sources of distress for Mr. Patel. At home, even the sound of a door slamming or an abrupt movement from his wife can cause him to startle and react as if he were in immediate danger. This heightened state of alertness has led to tension within their marriage. He often finds himself withdrawing from social activities and avoiding situations where such sounds might occur. Mr. Patel’s memories of the accident are predominantly visual, replaying like a film in his mind with every detail vividly clear. The sight of shattered glass and the intense feeling of helplessness during the collision persistently intrude into his daily life. When he recalls the event, it feels as though he is reliving it right then and there, experiencing the same terror and panic he felt on that fateful night. Despite these overwhelming symptoms, Mr. Patel has managed to hold onto his job out of a sense of duty and responsibility to his community. However, his work performance has declined over time as he struggles with concentration and anxiety. The cumulative stress has led to strained relationships at work, with colleagues noticing his frequent absences from meetings and his growing isolation. It was the realization that these symptoms were beginning to interfere significantly with both his professional and personal life that finally pushed Mr. Patel to seek help. He had come to believe that he could no longer manage on his own and feared becoming increasingly isolated from those he cared about most. What frightened him most was the possibility of losing his ability to contribute meaningfully to his community, a role he deeply cherished. In seeking therapy, Mr. Patel hopes to regain control over his life and find ways to cope with the overwhelming triggers that have come to define much of his daily experience since the accident. He is eager to learn strategies to manage his flashbacks and startle reactions while also addressing the broader impact on his relationships and work life. His primary hope is to reclaim a sense of peace and normalcy, allowing him to continue serving his community without being constantly haunted by the traumatic event.
